extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, students of poetry, and serious readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative principles for assessing poetry and poetic prose—focusing on how well a work interprets nature and the moral world, the balance between sensuousness and intellect, the poet's temperament, and qualities of expression (language, rhythm, tone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as interpreter of the natural world (naturalistic interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry is the interpretress of the natural world ... To make magically near and real the life of Nature, and man's life only so far as it is a part of that Nature, was his faculty; a faculty of naturalistic, not of moral interpretation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how vividly and authentically the poem renders the outward world: does expression correspond to the thing's essential reality? This faculty often rests on a delicate temperament and 'passive' reception of impressions. Examples: Guérin and Keats are held up as masters of naturalistic interpretation. Anti-pattern: language that fails to make nature feel 'magically near.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as interpreter of the moral/spiritual world (moral profundity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry also "interprets by expressing, with inspired conviction, the ideas and laws of the inward world of man's moral and spiritual nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the poem expresses moral/spiritual insight that gives readers a satisfying sense of human meaning and reconciles man with himself and the universe. Examples cited include Aeschylus and Shakespeare. This is a distinct but complementary interpretative mode to natural depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between natural and moral interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: "These great poets unite in themselves the faculty of both kinds of interpretation, the naturalistic and the moral. But ... the latter (the moral) usually ends by making itself the master."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poet successfully balances sensuous/natural rendering with moral/intellectual reflection. The critic warns that moral interpretation often comes to dominate; Shakespeare manages a near-balance (but leans), while Wordsworth and Lucretius tilt moral. Shelley strives for both but often fails to achieve natural magic in language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural magic of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: "The natural magic is perfect; when they speak of the world they speak like Adam naming by divine inspiration the creatures; their expression corresponds with the thing's essential reality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a correspondence between word-choice and the object's essence — an almost naming or evocation of reality. Keats and Guérin exemplify this. Contrast: Shelley may have rhythmic magic but lacks this language-based natural magic (examples and judgments invoked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic temperament: delicacy, susceptibility, and passivity
rubrics_metrics.description: A naturalistic faculty 'always has for its basis a peculiar temperament, an extraordinary delicacy of organisation and susceptibility to impressions; in exercising it the poet is in a great degree passive (Wordsworth thus speaks of a wise passiveness).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how the poet's temperament (sensitivity, receptivity to impressions, tendency to brood) contributes to the work's success. The temperament enables fine natural description but may incline the poet away from active moral agency or public career. Evaluate whether passivity yields authentic impression or mere self-indulgence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding over-intellectualisation; preserving sensuous simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Expression tends to become too little sensuous and simple, too much intellectualised."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique any tendency to sacrifice immediate sensuous detail for abstract intellectualisation. The best work maintains sensory immediacy; over-intellectualized diction can weaken natural magic. Shakespeare is praised for balancing but warned of occasional intellectualisation; maintain sensuous simplicity where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and musical power versus mastery of language
rubrics_metrics.description: "I will not deny ... that Shelley has natural magic in his rhythm; what I deny is, that he has it in his language. It always seems to me that the right sphere for Shelley's genius was the sphere of music, not of poetry; the medium of sounds he can master, but to master the more difficult medium of words he has neither intellectual force enough nor sanity enough."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate evaluation of rhythmic/musical gifts from precision and natural magic of diction. A poet may excel in rhythm (musicality) yet fail to achieve exact, evocative language. Judge both dimensions independently and note where rhythm compensates or fails to compensate for linguistic weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfectionism, secrecy, and the decision to publish
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is more power and beauty in the well-kept secret of one's self and one's thoughts, than in the display of a whole heaven that one may have inside one." (Guérin's reluctance to publish.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider an author's attitude to publication and perfectionism: restraint or refusal to publish may be ethically/artistically defensible if rooted in a pursuit of perfection, but it also limits public influence. The critic discusses the torture of needing constantly to produce vs. keeping a well-kept secret; evaluate effects on the body of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and authenticity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: "When I have finished, I see nothing but a wretched made-up imitation, composed of odds and ends of colour stolen from other people's palettes, and tastelessly mixed together on mine."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work feels derivative or genuinely original. Watch for piecemeal borrowing and 'tasteless' mixing of others' effects. Authentic, felicitous expression is a mark of mastery; imitation is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's reconciliatory function (giving a satisfying sense of reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry "gives him a satisfying sense of reality; it reconciles him with himself and the universe."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poem provides a unifying, reconciling perspective—whether through natural or moral interpretation it restores a sense of coherence and reality to the reader. This is a central criterion of poetic value in the essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity of temperament: artistic brilliance vs personal cost
rubrics_metrics.description: The temperament 'uses vital power too hard and too fast, paying the penalty in long hours of unutterable exhaustion and in premature death.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that extreme intensity can produce unique brilliance (distinctive 'flavour') but often at heavy personal cost (morbid exhaustion, early death). Evaluate both the aesthetic fruit and the evident human toll reflected in the work or biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as experiencer rather than moral agent
rubrics_metrics.description: "He goes into religion and out of religion, into society and out of society, not from the motives which impel men in general, but to feel what it is all like; he is thus hardly a moral agent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a poet, note whether the impulse is to apprehend and render experience rather than to act or argue morally. This disposition can produce finely observed, interior work but may lack overt moral agency or practical engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone/voice: sensuous-genial versus mystic-inward
rubrics_metrics.description: "Keats has, above all, a sense of what is pleasurable and open in the life of nature ... genial, outward, and sensuous. Guérin has, above all, a sense of what there is adorable and secret in the life of Nature ... mystic, inward, and profound."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the poem's tone and voice align with its aims: an outward, sensuous tone suits certain natural renderings; a mystic, inward tone suits secret, devotional or contemplative renderings. This is a stylistic axis—neither is superior per se, but suitability and execution matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mythic/prose-poem forms to channel natural magic
rubrics_metrics.description: The Centaur (a prose-poem) 'has in a wonderful degree that natural magic ... and the rhythm has a charm which bewitches even a foreigner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the effectiveness of mythic or hybrid forms (prose-poem, mythic narrative) in producing natural magic and rhythmic charm. Such forms can be especially apt for evoking the life of Nature and the visionary imagination if executed with felicitous language and rhythm.
